clue.text: A place for fun when it's out of bounds!

definitions.text: A place for fun when it's out of bounds!

blocks.clueFragment: A place for fun when it's out of bounds!
blocks.note: surface reading: somewhere enjoyable that is off limits, forbidden territory
setter's reading: the fun comes while you are up in the air after bouncing, bounds meaning leaps

explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of bounds' normally means forbidden; here bounds are springy leaps, and the fun happens between them on a gymnastic bed of canvas and springs.
explanation.definitionFit: A trampoline is a stretched sheet on springs where people bounce for recreation, so it is a play spot defined by its leaps.

clue.text: Hackneyed ceremony after the end of August

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, the only one kept

blocks.note: the final letter of the month's name
a rite is a ceremony

explanation.surface: A tired old ceremony held at the close of summer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the ceremony after the letter, so the letter comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Trite means overused and stale through repetition, the same sense as hackneyed.

clue.text: Great menu set out, yet he will add something to it

definitions.text: he will add something to it

indicators.note: setting things out arranges them afresh, so the letters are laid out in a new order

blocks.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: A splendid menu is laid out, yet some diner still wants to add an extra dish.
explanation.definitionFit: An augmenter is one who increases or supplements things, so he is a person who enlarges what is there.

clue.text: Plain yellow or mottled grouse

blocks.note: a prairie is a grassy plain
yellow and chicken both mean cowardly

explanation.surface: A birder debates whether a grouse is plain yellow or speckled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' and 'yellow' look like colour descriptions of the bird; one is a grassland and the other means cowardly.
explanation.definitionFit: The prairie chicken is a North American bird of the grouse family with barred brown plumage.

clue.text: Weapon of Little John or Tall Bob, say?

blocks.note: tall and long both describe great length
a bob is a quick bow or curtsey, so it is an example of one

explanation.surface: Robin Hood's giant companion Little John, ironically named, might as well be called Tall Bob.
explanation.walkthrough: Bob looks like a name; it is a little bob of the head or knee.
explanation.definitionFit: The longbow was the tall English archery weapon carried by Robin Hood's outlaws, Little John among them.

clue.text: The last place to see Society looking threadbare

blocks.note: from the saying see Naples and die, so it is the last sight before death
S is the abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: The final venue where fashionable society might be seen is looking worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'See Naples and die' means the Italian city is so beautiful there is nothing left to see after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Napless cloth has lost its raised surface fibres through wear, so it is worn and shabby.

clue.text: Common fog is half soot, travelling northwards

indicators.note: half of a four-letter word means keeping just two of its letters, here the front pair

blocks.note: the first half of the word soot
going north is going up the map

explanation.surface: A grimy smog, half of it soot, drifts north across the town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Travelling northwards' looks like a reversal signal in a down clue, but this is an across entry and the phrase simply supplies UP. 'Pea soup' is old slang for thick London fog.
explanation.definitionFit: A dense yellowish smog was nicknamed a pea-souper, so soup is informal slang for thick fog.

clue.text: Ring that contains a magpie?

blocks.note: surface reading: a bird ring or a circle with a black and white bird inside
setter's reading: in target shooting a magpie is a shot landing in the ring just inside the edge of the target

explanation.walkthrough: A magpie is old marksmen's slang for a hit on the target ring next to the outermost, so it lies in this zone.
explanation.definitionFit: On an archery or rifle target this is the broad band furthest from the bull, the edge zone of scoring circles.

clue.text: Elderly retired, in overcrowded environment, well secured

indicators.note: retired means drawn back, so the word is read backwards
in puts one word inside the environment named next

blocks.note: a packed place is overcrowded; environment says it surrounds the other piece
elderly means old

explanation.surface: An old pensioner, retired to a crowded home, is safely locked in.
explanation.definitionFit: Something padlocked is fastened with a detachable lock through a staple, so it is firmly fastened shut.

clue.text: Henry Higgins was one egotistical old sort!

indicators.note: sort works as a verb here, meaning to arrange the preceding letters differently

blocks.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: Professor Higgins of Pygmalion is called a vain old fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort' looks like a noun for a type of person, but it is the anagram signal. Higgins, in Shaw's Pygmalion, is a phonetics professor who identifies people by their accents.
explanation.definitionFit: A dialectologist studies regional varieties of speech, which is exactly the expertise Shaw gave his phonetics professor.

clue.text: Dye made from iodine, no good against showers

blocks.note: I is the chemical symbol for iodine
NG is the common abbreviation for no good
showers are falls of rain

explanation.surface: A dyestuff made from iodine fails to hold up against wet weather.
explanation.definitionFit: To ingrain is an old textile verb for colouring fibres thoroughly before weaving, so it means to dye fast.

clue.text: Edged as old brickwork joints should be?

definitions.text: as old brickwork joints should be?

blocks.note: first meaning: having a sharp tip or edge

blocks.clueFragment: as old brickwork joints should be?
blocks.note: second meaning: mortar between bricks that has been renewed by a builder

explanation.walkthrough: Pointing is the building trade's word for raking out and refilling the mortar between bricks, which old walls periodically need.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means sharp-tipped, and is also the past participle builders use for walls whose mortar seams have been refreshed.

clue.text: English river shellfish the French find abhorrent

blocks.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, England
a crab is a shellfish
le is French for the

explanation.surface: French diners turn up their noses at shellfish taken from an English river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Exe is a river in south-west England flowing through Exeter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something execrable is utterly detestable, a close synonym for loathsome or abhorrent.

clue.text: Longship slow in the air?

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for long
the Argo was Jason's ship in Greek myth

explanation.surface: A Viking longship drifts slowly through the air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Longship' must be split into two words. The air here is a tune, not the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Largo is the musical tempo marking for a broad, very unhurried pace, so it describes a slow melody.

clue.text: Western eminence flatter? Not right

indicators.note: not right says the abbreviation for right must be dropped from the word

blocks.note: to butter someone up is to flatter them

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether praising a Western dignitary is just flattery, and is told no.
explanation.walkthrough: R stands for right, so BUTTER loses its R. 'Eminence' is a high piece of ground, not a cardinal.
explanation.definitionFit: A butte is an isolated flat-topped hill typical of the American West, so it is a high landform there.

clue.text: One's first calling-place?

blocks.note: surface reading: the first place a salesman or visitor calls in at
setter's reading: where a baby is first called by name, at the christening font

explanation.walkthrough: Calling suggests visiting or a vocation; here it is being given a name at a christening, the first time anyone calls you anything.
explanation.definitionFit: A baptistry is the part of a church holding the font, where infants are christened and formally given their names.

clue.text: Knowing cocaine makes one gag ..

blocks.note: knowing in the sense of shrewd or worldly
crack is a form of cocaine

explanation.surface: Knowingly taking cocaine leaves someone choking.
explanation.walkthrough: Gag looks like a verb for retching, but it is a noun meaning a joke. The dots carry the thought into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A wisecrack is a smart, flippant quip, so it is a kind of joke or comic line.

clue.text: Cor! a happy outcome of some old books

indicators.note: an outcome is what results when the given letters are worked into something new

blocks.note: the letters of the exclamation, the article and the adjective

explanation.surface: A delighted reader exclaims at the happy ending of some old books.
explanation.definitionFit: The Apocrypha are ancient scriptural writings left out of the Hebrew Bible canon, so they are a set of old texts.

clue.text: ... through providence, possibly?

blocks.note: per is Latin for through, as in per annum
fate or luck, what providence brings

explanation.surface: Following the previous clue's gag, it may have come about through providence.
explanation.definitionFit: Perchance is an old-fashioned adverb meaning perhaps, so it can replace possibly in a sentence.

clue.text: Two races recognised by Disraeli

blocks.note: surface reading: a pair of horse races or ethnic groups a prime minister acknowledged
setter's reading: his novel Sybil, subtitled for the rich and the poor of England as two peoples

explanation.walkthrough: Benjamin Disraeli, Victorian novelist and prime minister, subtitled his novel Sybil 'The Two Nations', meaning the rich and the poor.
explanation.definitionFit: Nations means peoples or races, and Disraeli famously described England's rich and poor as separate peoples.

clue.text: Banging drums may aggravate it

blocks.note: surface reading: a loud percussionist annoys the neighbours
setter's reading: the drums are eardrums, and banging on them makes an ache worse

explanation.walkthrough: Drums suggests a drum kit; it is the eardrum, and loud noise worsens pain there.
explanation.definitionFit: Earache is pain inside the ear, which loud noise striking the eardrums can make worse.

clue.text: Nothing unoccupied at the Oval

blocks.note: O looks like zero, nothing
empty, unoccupied

explanation.surface: Empty seats at the Oval cricket ground on a quiet day.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oval is a London cricket ground; the capital letter tempts you to read it as a place, but it is an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovoid means egg-shaped, an adjective covering much the same rounded elongated shape as oval.

clue.text: One icon broken in classical style

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, so its letters can be put back in another order

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A single religious icon lies smashed amid classical ruins.
explanation.definitionFit: Ionic is one of the classical Greek orders of architecture, recognised by scroll-shaped column capitals.

clue.text: Marshal holds bible on edge

indicators.note: holds means one word grips the other inside it

blocks.note: Michel Ney was one of Napoleon's marshals
RV is the Revised Version of the Bible

explanation.surface: A nervous marshal clutches his bible.
explanation.walkthrough: The marshal is Napoleon's Marshal Ney, a stock crossword figure; the Revised Version is an English Bible translation of the 1880s.
explanation.definitionFit: Nervy in British usage means jittery or anxious, so it describes someone who is on edge.

clue.text: Tailless flatfish approaching shore like an aircraft

indicators.note: without a tail means the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: a turbot is a flatfish
to shore up is to prop, a shore being a support

explanation.surface: A fish missing its tail swims towards the beach, gliding like a plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shore' looks like the seaside, but here it is a timber prop holding up a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: A turboprop is a plane whose propeller is driven by a gas turbine engine, a common type of airliner.

clue.text: Bets in Irish pounds

blocks.note: first meaning: wagers placed by a gambler
second meaning: the currency of Ireland before the euro

explanation.surface: A gambler places wagers in Irish money.
explanation.walkthrough: The punt was the Irish pound, replaced by the euro in 2002.
explanation.definitionFit: A punter makes wagers, so punts are bets; the Irish currency unit was also called the punt.

clue.text: Threat from low tars coming out of the tube

definitions.text: Threat from low tars coming out of the tube

blocks.clueFragment: Threat from low tars coming out of the tube
blocks.note: surface reading: menacing sailors emerging from the London Underground
setter's reading: tars are sailors and low ones are submariners, whose weapon is fired from a launching tube

explanation.walkthrough: The tube looks like the London Underground; it is the launching tube of a submarine, and tars is slang for sailors.
explanation.definitionFit: A torpedo is the self-propelled underwater missile that a submarine fires at ships, a serious danger to them.

clue.text: Criminal snared by the wire?

blocks.note: surface reading: a burglar caught on barbed wire or a trip wire
setter's reading: a wireless telegraph message sent to a ship led to the arrest

explanation.walkthrough: In 1910 the murderer Dr Crippen fled to Canada by ship and was the first criminal caught with the help of a wireless telegram.
explanation.definitionFit: Hawley Crippen was an infamous Edwardian poisoner, the first fugitive arrested thanks to a radio message sent to the liner.

clue.text: Toy swing

blocks.note: first meaning: a spool spun up and down on a string
second meaning: to fluctuate up and down repeatedly

explanation.definitionFit: The noun names a string plaything, and the verb describes prices or moods rising and falling repeatedly.

clue.text: Translating "to be" - Latin's basic elements

indicators.note: translating carries words into a new form, so it also signals the second word being rearranged

blocks.note: esse is the Latin infinitive meaning to be
the letters of the word, possessive s included

explanation.surface: A schoolroom exercise: rendering 'to be' into Latin, the basics of the language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Translating' does two jobs: it puts 'to be' into Latin, and it rearranges the letters of Latin's.
explanation.definitionFit: Essentials are the fundamental, indispensable parts of something, so the word means its basic components.
